summary:
Martian Route: survival routes for human walks on Mars

On a Martian walk, the limit is not distance but the oxygen the explorer carries. Between the base and a target lie scarps, boulder fields and loose sand. Curiosity has had to adapt its drives for years, and a short route up a steep slope can cost a person more oxygen than a detour and leave no margin to return.

Martian Route is a multilayer 3D map of Jezero crater that plans human EVAs on foot. The explorer picks a start and a destination and receives three routes (Safe, Fast and Science), compared with the shortest path that respects the slope limit. Each route reports its oxygen use per person, risk, time, radiation dose and the point of no return. A safe-return map colors the terrain green, yellow or red depending on whether the explorer can get back within the suit’s autonomy, needs the reserve, or cannot return.

The tool combines public NASA data on a common grid of about 25 m:

CTX terrain model and orthomosaic (MRO).
NOAH-H terrain classes from HiRISE, covering 95.4 % of the area.
THEMIS thermal inertia (Mars Odyssey).
Perseverance’s real traverse, for validation.
Curiosity RAD dose rates.
Live DONKI space-weather alerts.

Every figure in the app shows its source and whether it is observed, derived or modeled.
details:
What it does. Martian Route is a web planner for walking EVAs on Mars. On a 3D model of Jezero crater built from real orbital data, the explorer picks a start and a destination. The engine returns three routes (Safe, Fast and Science) plus a baseline: the shortest path that respects the suit’s slope limit. Each route reports oxygen per person as a range, EVA time in hours and sols, radiation dose, average terrain risk, the point of no return and the difference against the baseline. A safe-return map colors the whole area by the time needed to walk back to base: green within the plannable autonomy, yellow only using the reserve, red with no return. A “Mars today” panel adds live NASA context: solar eruptions forecast to reach Mars (DONKI) and Perseverance’s latest position and raw images.

Try in real time in: https://martian-route.vercel.app/

How it works.

  1. An offline pipeline (Python, Rasterio/GDAL) brings NASA and USGS products to a common 600 × 600 grid of ~25 m. From them it derives slope, terrain risk (NOAH-H classes on HiRISE) and ground instability (THEMIS thermal inertia), with coverage and provenance for each layer.
  2. A route engine (FastAPI, NumPy, scikit-image) combines the layers into a cost per cell with weights for each mode. It treats slopes above the suit limit as impassable and finds the minimum-cost path. Oxygen follows the slope-cost curve of Minetti et al. (2002), bounded between two gravity assumptions, because there are no suited walking data at 0.38 g.
  3. A 3D viewer (Next.js, React Three Fiber) shows the terrain, the data layers, the routes, the Perseverance traverse and a comparison table, in English and Spanish.

Results on real Jezero data (demo scenario). The Safe route has 66 % less obstacle risk than the shortest path, at a cost of +0.8 km and +0.03 kg of O₂ per person. 44 % of the area allows a return to base within the plannable 3.2 h.

Why it matters. Mars data viewers measure; rover planners optimize the rover. A PRISMA 2020 review of 97 studies found no tool that plans a walk for a person on Mars by oxygen and safe return, using real data. Martian Route puts real Mars layers, oxygen cost and safe return in one workflow.

What makes it different. Safety works as a constraint, not just a weight. Oxygen is shown as a range, not a single number. Every figure carries its source and a tag: observed, derived or modeled. The suit limits are editable.

Impact. EVA planning for future crewed missions, crew training in Earth analogs, and outreach with real NASA data. The method is open and repeatable: Gale crater is already built as a second site.

Tools. Python, TypeScript, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, Rasterio/GDAL, Next.js, React Three Fiber, three.js, Docker, Vercel, Render and GitHub Actions.

Limits we state openly. Oxygen cost is calibrated with lunar and Earth data. The radiation rate was measured at Gale, not Jezero. Validation against Perseverance’s traverse and user tests are still pending.
